```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# B and n_range only affect the legacy per-arm Monte Carlo fields of
# bam_sample_size(); the exact result does not depend on them.
options(dtasamplesize.warn_small_B = FALSE)
```

This vignette follows the planning of a validation study of a rapid antigen
test from a published pilot, with the exact Bayesian assurance method of
`bam_sample_size()` (Wilson et al. 2022; Williamson et al. 2023). Every count
comes from two published articles; nothing here is simulated. The complete
analysis, with finer grids, the local Hellinger sensitivity and all the
tables, is in `validation/applied_example.R` of the source repository
(output: log, CSV tables and figure).

## The data

* **Pilot** (Albert et al. 2021, *Clin Microbiol Infect* 27:472.e7-e10,
  [doi:10.1016/j.cmi.2020.11.004](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmi.2020.11.004)):
  Panbio COVID-19 Ag rapid test against RT-PCR in 412 symptomatic patients of
  primary care centres in Valencia, Spain. Counts: TP = 43, FN = 11, FP = 0,
  TN = 358 (single-gate cohort; prevalence 54/412 = 13.1%). FP = 0 is
  derived from the printed totals.
* **Validation study** (Bulilete et al. 2021, *J Infect* 82:391-398,
  [doi:10.1016/j.jinf.2021.02.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinf.2021.02.014)):
  the same test in 1362 analysed adults in primary care in Mallorca. Counts:
  TP = 100, FN = 40, FP = 2, TN = 1220. The authors planned 927 participants
  with a frequentist calculation (prevalence 15%, error 5%, sensitivity 90%)
  and enrolled 1369.

```{r data}
pilot <- list(tp = 43, fn = 11, tn = 358, fp = 0)
valid <- list(tp = 100, fn = 40, tn = 1220, fp = 2)
library(dtasamplesize)
```

We plan the validation study as if it had not been done yet, and use its
counts only at the end, for the post-study conflict check. The study sizes
are always *total* sample sizes (diseased plus non-diseased).

## Initial prior and its compatibility with the pilot

The base case uses a flat Beta(1, 1) initial prior for sensitivity (Se),
specificity (Sp) and prevalence. **The compatibility check between the
initial prior and the pilot is not informative with a flat prior**: with
Beta(1, 1) the prior predictive distribution is uniform and the smallest
attainable tail probability is 1/(n + 1), so only extreme results can be
flagged, and a flag only says that the count is extreme, not that it
contradicts a flat prior, which predicts nothing specific. The function
says so:

```{r flat-check}
invisible(tryCatch(
  bam_prior_data_conflict(tp = 43, fn = 11, tn = 358, fp = 0,
                          prior_se = c(1, 1), prior_sp = c(1, 1)),
  warning = function(w) cat("Warning:", conditionMessage(w), "\n")))
```

The check is useful when the initial prior is informative. As a secondary
illustration, take an initial prior centred on the manufacturer's claims
quoted by Bulilete et al. (Se 93.3%, Sp 99.4%) with an **illustrative
effective size of 10 observations per arm** (an assumption of this example,
not a published value):

```{r manuf-check}
m_se <- c(0.933, 0.067) * 10
m_sp <- c(0.994, 0.006) * 10
chk <- bam_prior_data_conflict(tp = 43, fn = 11, tn = 358, fp = 0,
                               prior_se = m_se, prior_sp = m_sp)
as.data.frame(chk)[, c("quantity", "x_obs", "n", "p_lower", "p_upper",
                       "p_two_sided", "flag_two_sided")]
```

The observed sensitivity of the pilot (43 of 54) falls in the lower tail of
what that initial prior predicts (lower-tail probability
`r sprintf("%.3f", as.data.frame(chk)$p_lower[1])`): it is not flagged at the
0.05 threshold, but it is close, and a more concentrated initial prior (an
effective size of 20 gives 0.049) would flag it. Specificity (358 of 358) is
fully compatible. This is the kind of reading the check supports: review the
initial prior (or the claim behind it). **What this check does not tell us**: it says nothing about how much weight
the pilot should receive in the design prior (the heterogeneity between the
pilot and the future study is not observed when planning), and a conflict
does not say which source is wrong. It is a review of the *initial* prior,
nothing more. The rest of the vignette uses the flat initial prior.

## Design and analysis priors from the pilot

`bam_prior_from_pilot()` updates the Beta priors with the pilot counts using
a power prior with a fixed weight `a0` in (0, 1]. The choice of `a0` rests on
the similarity of the populations, not on the conflict check. Here the
pilot enrolled only symptomatic patients, including children, whereas the
validation study enrolled adults only and more than half were close contacts
(many asymptomatic, with lower sensitivity). Same test, sample type,
operators, reference test and country, in contiguous periods: the populations
are partly similar, so we take `a0 = 0.5` as the base value and explore
0.25 and 1 below.

The *analysis* prior is the one used to compute the posterior interval once the
new study's data are in. With `use_in = "design"` the updated prior is used only to
generate the data and the analysis starts from the flat base prior (the
new study is analysed without borrowing the pilot; this is the principal choice
here). With `use_in = "both"` the updated prior is also the analysis prior.

```{r priors}
pri <- function(a0, use_in) do.call(bam_prior_from_pilot, c(pilot, list(
  base_prior_se = c(1, 1), base_prior_sp = c(1, 1), base_prior_prev = c(1, 1),
  a0 = a0, use_in = use_in)))
p_des  <- pri(0.5, "design")
p_both <- pri(0.5, "both")
p_des
```

## Exact sample size

The width targets are those used by Williamson et al. (2023) in their
illustrative example, from the MHRA target product profile: lower one-sided
semi-widths of 0.10 for Se and 0.05 for Sp (posterior median minus the
one-sided 95% lower bound, `width_type = "lower_half_width"`), joint
objective, assurance 0.80. `bam_sensitivity()` evaluates a list of
scenarios exactly (no simulation) and returns one row per scenario with
the smallest total `N_total`, `A_N` and `A_N_minus_1`. We add a two-sided
alternative (95% equal-tailed interval, full widths 0.20 and 0.10, that is
twice the one-sided semi-widths: a convention, not an equivalence) and the
`use_in = "both"` variant.

```{r sizes}
two <- list(width_type = "full_width", delta_se = 0.20, delta_sp = 0.10)
scen <- list(
  design_onesided_joint = list(priors = p_des),
  both_onesided_joint   = list(priors = p_both),
  design_twosided_joint = c(list(priors = p_des), two),
  a0_0.25 = list(priors = pri(0.25, "design")),
  a0_1    = list(priors = pri(1, "design")))
tab <- withCallingHandlers(
  bam_sensitivity(scen, delta_se = 0.10, delta_sp = 0.05,
    width_type = "lower_half_width", alpha_ci = 0.95, target_assurance = 0.80),
  warning = function(w) {
    cat("Warning:", conditionMessage(w), "\n\n")
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
tab[, c("scenario", "N_total", "A_N", "A_N_minus_1")]
```

```{r sizes-values, include = FALSE}
n_main <- tab$N_total[tab$scenario == "design_onesided_joint"]
n_both <- tab$N_total[tab$scenario == "both_onesided_joint"]
```

The principal scenario recommends `r n_main` participants, to be compared with
the 927 planned (frequentist) and the 1369 enrolled by Bulilete et al. With
`use_in = "both"` the recommendation falls to `r n_both`, but this is because
the updated Sp prior (concentrated near 1 after FP = 0) already meets the Sp
width before any data are observed, so the Sp criterion stops constraining N
and success depends on the prior. `bam_sensitivity()` warns about it (the warning
is printed above the table). This is why `use_in = "design"` is
the principal choice. Marginal objectives (for example `assurance_for = "se"`)
and the full tables are in `validation/applied_example.R`.

## Sensitivity

The rows `a0_0.25` and `a0_1` above are the sensitivity to the pilot weight.
Other sensitivities (width targets, assurance target, prior of prevalence, for
example one centred on the 15% assumed by Bulilete et al.) are one more
scenario each in the same list. The local sensitivity to the *initial* prior
by Hellinger distance, `bam_sensitivity_local()`, perturbs the initial prior
along a contour of fixed distance `epsilon`, re-applies the pilot and reports
the range of the assurance and of N; it is slow, so it is not evaluated in
this vignette:

```{r hellinger, eval = FALSE}
bam_sensitivity_local(
  base_prior_se = c(1, 1), base_prior_sp = c(1, 1), base_prior_prev = c(1, 1),
  which = "se", epsilon = 0.01, n_phi = 24, pilot = pilot, a0 = 0.5,
  use_in = "design", n_ref = n_main,
  delta_se = 0.10, delta_sp = 0.05, width_type = "lower_half_width")
```

The exact assurance curve of the principal scenario shows how the target is
reached (the figure of `validation/applied_example.R` adds the curves for
other values of `a0` and for `use_in = "both"`):

```{r curve, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
Nr <- seq(50, 1000, by = 10)
cv <- bam_assurance_curve(priors = p_des, N_range = c(Nr, n_main),
  delta_se = 0.10, delta_sp = 0.05, width_type = "lower_half_width")
plot(cv$curve$N, cv$curve$assurance, type = "l", lwd = 2, las = 1,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Total sample size N", ylab = "Exact assurance A(N)")
abline(h = 0.80, col = "grey50", lty = 5)
abline(v = 927, col = "grey30", lty = 3)
points(n_main, tab$A_N[1], pch = 19)
```

The dotted vertical marks the 927 participants planned by Bulilete et al.
(1369 were enrolled, beyond the range drawn) and the dashed horizontal line
the target.

## Frequentist complement with fixed values

Buderer's formula needs point values. The pilot gives Se = 43/54 and
prevalence 54/412, but its Sp is 1 (FP = 0) and the formula degenerates, so we
fix a plausible declared value: the lower limit of the two-sided 95% Wilson
interval of the pilot Sp (358 of 358). This is a choice of the example.

```{r buderer}
se <- 43 / 54; prev <- 54 / 412
sp <- unname(wilson_ci(358, 358, alpha = 0.05)["lower"])
nd <- buderer_n(se, 0.10, alpha = 0.10)   # one-sided 95%: z = qnorm(0.95)
nn <- buderer_n(sp, 0.05, alpha = 0.10)
c(Sp_fixed = sp, n_diseased = nd, n_non_diseased = nn,
  N_total = max(ceiling(nd / prev), ceiling(nn / (1 - prev))))
```

This number ignores the uncertainty about Se, Sp and prevalence and the
probability that the realised interval meets the target, so it is not the
same question as the assurance: it is a reference point, not a competitor.
The 927 of Bulilete et al. is reproduced with Buderer's formula for the Se
arm and their declared inputs (`ceiling(buderer_n(0.90, 0.05) / 0.15)`),
without claiming that this was the formula they used.

## Post-study conflict check with the validation data

Once the study is done, `bam_prior_data_conflict()` compares its counts with
the prior predictive distributions: the number of diseased (prevalence
prior), true positives among the diseased (Se prior) and true negatives
among the non-diseased (Sp prior). For Se and Sp it returns two references:
the predictive of the **analysis prior** (the inferential reference: does the
prior used to analyse the data agree with them?) and that of the **design
prior** (calibration of the assurance: were the data generated as the
planning assumed?). The prevalence row refers to the design prior, because
there is no analysis prior for prevalence.

```{r post-conflict}
post <- bam_prior_data_conflict(tp = 100, fn = 40, tn = 1220, fp = 2,
                                priors = p_des)
as.data.frame(post)[, c("quantity", "reference", "x_obs", "n", "p_lower",
                        "p_upper", "p_two_sided", "flag_two_sided")]
```

With `use_in = "design"` the analysis prior is flat, so the rows against
the analysis prior are weak checks (the flat-prior warning applies: with
Beta(1, 1) the predictive is uniform and only extreme results are flagged;
here the specificity row, 1220 of 1222 against a uniform predictive, is
flagged in its upper tail, which reflects the flatness of the prior rather
than a difference between the pilot and the validation study). The rows against the **design prior** are the
calibration of the assurance: none is flagged. The observed sensitivity
(100/140, 71.4%) is lower than the pilot's (79.6%), but it lies within what
the design prior predicted (lower-tail probability about 0.23 at `a0` = 0.5),
and the prevalence (140 of 1362, 10.3%) is also compatible with the design
prior (lower tail about 0.10). So the planning assumptions were not
contradicted by the new data. As with the planning check, a conflict (or its
absence) does not say which source is at fault, and the check is not used to
choose `a0`. With `use_in = "both"` the analysis and design priors coincide
and a single row per quantity is returned.

* Albert E, et al. Field evaluation of a rapid antigen test (Panbio COVID-19 Ag
  Rapid Test Device) for COVID-19 diagnosis in primary healthcare centres.
  *Clin Microbiol Infect* 2021;27:472.e7-e10.
  [doi:10.1016/j.cmi.2020.11.004](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmi.2020.11.004)
* Bulilete O, et al. Panbio rapid antigen test for SARS-CoV-2 has acceptable
  accuracy in symptomatic patients in primary health care. *J Infect*
  2021;82:391-398.
  [doi:10.1016/j.jinf.2021.02.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinf.2021.02.014)
* Wilson KJ, et al. Bayesian sample size determination for diagnostic accuracy
  studies. *Stat Med* 2022;41:2908-2922.
  [doi:10.1002/sim.9393](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.9393)
* Williamson SF, et al. Sample size determination for point-of-care COVID-19
  diagnostic tests: a Bayesian approach. *Diagn Progn Res* 2023;7:17.
